newsitem.title: Cuba: Cuba stages rare military parade.
newsitem.headline: Cuba stages rare military parade.

text.p: Thousands of officers, soldiers and civilian militia members marched through Havana on Monday as Cuba staged a rare military parade to mark the 40th anniversary of the founding of its Revolutionary Armed Forces.

President Fidel Castro and Defence Minister Raul Castro, his younger brother, presided over the event in Revolution Square, which was officially presented as reaffirming the country's communist system and showing Cuba is prepared to meet any military threat.

It was the largest such parade in the city since the collapse of Cuba's old economic and military partner, the former Soviet Union. Reflecting austere economic times, the parade was on foot and a flyover by the air force consisted of just three Soviet-made MiG-29 fighter aircraft.

Tanks such as the Soviet-made T-72, armoured vehicles, planes such as the MiG-23 and MiG-29, helicopters and artillery were displayed in a standing exhibit in the square rather than being rolled past, to save fuel.
"Loyal to this revolution, we made it together and we will defend it together," Gen. Rafael Hernandez Delgado said. "We reaffirm that the spirit of resistance will be immortal."

Workers in Havana were given a day's holiday to mark the event. Dec. 2, 1956 was the day when Fidel Castro, then 30, disembarked with some 82 rebels from the boat Granma in eastern Cuba to launch the guerrilla war that toppled dictator Fulgencio Batista in January 1959.

Raul Castro said in a newspaper interview published on Monday that Cuba still faced a threat from the United States from those who wanted to provoke civil disorder to justify military invasion. Despite the difficulties after the Soviet collapse, he said Cuba was still prepared to face any threat.

But he also told the weekly trade union newspaper Trabajadores Cuba that U.S. military leaders were aware that "firstly Cuba constitutes no threat to the national security of the United States, secondly that the price to pay in U.S. lives would be very high."

Horsemen recalling Cuba's 19-century independence wars against Spain were followed by some 3,000 school children accompanying a replica of the Granma through the square at the head of parade. Groups representing veterans of the 1956-59 guerrilla struggle, the troops who defeated CIA-backed Cuban exiles at the Bay of Pigs in 1961 and Cubans who took part in foreign wars including in Angola in the 1980s also filed past.

Official commentators stressed the Cuban-made weaponry featured in the parade -- the "Alejandro" rifle designed for snipers and an anti-helicopter gun called "Mambi," and the Cuban-made version of the Kalashnikov assault rifle. A television commentator said there were some 100,000 trained snipers in the country.
